summary: This document specifies the information in a conceptual database of long-lived cryptographic keys used by many routing protocols for message security. It supports both manual and automated key management and describes the database schema.

eli5.summary: Routers need many secret keys. This describes a tidy notebook for keeping them with all the needed details.

questions: what is the long-lived key database
what fields are in the routing key table
how are routing protocol keys selected
what is a kdf in key table
subtitle: A conceptual table that holds the long-lived secret keys routing protocols use, so key management and protocols stay separate.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols each handled their own authentication keys, which made manual key management inconsistent between vendors and made automated key management hard to bolt on.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a conceptual table with one row per long-lived symmetric key and columns such as LocalKeyName, Peers, Protocol, KDF, AlgID, Key, Direction and send and accept lifetimes. It also defines how protocols select keys and what each protocol must specify to use the table.
tldr.outcome: Key management can be written once without knowing any security protocol, and protocols plug in by describing how they use a row. The RFC lists no initial protocol registrations.

today: RFC 7210 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose of the Key Database
sections.content:
RFC 7210 specifies the information kept in a conceptual database of long-lived cryptographic keys, used to key the authentication of routing protocols. The database is meant to separate protocol-specific details from both manual and automated key management.

Many implementation approaches are allowed. The point is to simplify specification and mixed-vendor deployments, and to avoid building knowledge of any security protocol into key management protocols.

The long-lived key is not always used directly. In many cases a key derivation function (KDF) produces short-lived keys from it; in other cases the security protocol uses the long-lived key as is. The design supports both.
sections.eli5: Instead of every router keeping its secrets in its own messy way, everyone agrees on one tidy notebook layout. Then the people who hand out secrets and the people who use them do not need to know each other's business.

sections.title: The Key Table Columns
sections.content:
The database is a table. Each row is one long-lived symmetric key, and normally each key has only one row. Several rows hold the same key value only when a key serves more than one purpose or is used with several KDFs. The field formats are chosen so that a plain-text editor can update them and every system displays them the same way.

  • AdminKeyName: a human-readable name. Routing protocols do not use it.
  • LocalKeyName: identifies the key when a message arrives, in a form the protocol defines (often a 16 or 32 bit integer).
  • PeerKeyName: the name of the key in an outgoing message. For group keys it is typically an empty string.
  • Peers: the peer systems (unicast) or groups that hold the key.
  • Interfaces: the interfaces where the key may be used, or all.
  • Protocol and ProtocolSpecificInfo: which routing protocol the key is for, and extra information it needs. That information MUST NOT be required to locate a key.
  • KDF and AlgID: how short-lived keys are derived (or none) and which algorithm is used.
  • Key: the key as a lowercase hexadecimal string.
  • Direction: in, out, both or disabled.
  • Four lifetime fields: the earliest and latest times, in UTC, for sending and for accepting with the key.
sections.eli5: Each line of the notebook says the secret's nickname, who shares it, where it works, what trick to use with it, and the dates it may be used.

sections.title: Key Selection and Rollover
sections.content:
To pick a key for an outgoing message, the protocol supplies its name (P) and a peer identifier (H), and optionally an interface (I). A row qualifies when Peers includes H, Protocol matches P, Interfaces includes I or all, Direction is out or both, and the current time lies between SendLifetimeStart and SendLifeTimeEnd.

If several rows qualify, for example during a key change, the RFC recommends choosing the key with the most recent SendLifetimeStart. Systems should also be able to select by algorithm preference to ease algorithm transitions.

To validate an incoming message, the protocol also supplies the key identifier (L). If one row matches, it is selected: one whose Direction is in or both, whose LocalKeyName is L, and whose accept lifetime covers the current time.

Lifetimes bind loosely. New security associations should not be set up outside the accept period, allowing some grace for clock skew, but an association already established is not directly affected when the lifetime passes. Implementations with long-lived associations should check the database periodically and roll over without tearing the association down.
sections.eli5: When a router needs a secret, it looks down the notebook for a line that matches who it is talking to and today's date. If two lines match, it picks the newest.

sections.title: What a Protocol Must Specify
sections.content:
A protocol that wants to use the table must say how it maps onto it. The RFC lists nine items: how to fill in an outgoing message from a row, how to find the peer identifier and LocalKeyName in an incoming one, how to verify a message, the form and validation rules for key names and for members of Peers, the supported algorithms and KDFs, the form of ProtocolSpecificInfo, the canonicalization rules, and whether support for Interfaces is required.

The form of the Interfaces field is shared by all protocols on an implementation. If a protocol must tell apart several instances over one interface, that belongs in its definition of peers.
sections.eli5: A routing protocol that wants to use the notebook has to fill in a short checklist saying how it reads each column.

sections.title: Textual Conventions and Operations
sections.content:
Integer key names are written as lowercase hexadecimal digits, most significant octet first, padded with leading zeros to the width of the protocol's key identifier field. Text key names should use ASCII where possible; otherwise they MUST be in a Unicode encoding. An AdminKeyName outside ASCII MUST be UTF-8 and SHOULD be normalized with Unicode Normalization Form KC. A key itself is a lowercase hexadecimal string, most significant octet first.

On operations, the RFC warns that keys whose valid periods do not overlap, or clocks that disagree, can leave systems unable to agree on a key. When installing keys one after another, operators should set SendLifetimeStart several hours after AcceptLifeTimeStart so there is overlap, and may use a longer overlap such as several days.
sections.eli5: Everyone writes the secrets and nicknames in the same style, so a note from one company works on another's equipment. Overlapping dates make sure nobody is locked out during a swap.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls key management a significant operational problem, for both synchronization and selection. It cites RFC 3562, which warns against sharing TCP MD5 keying material between systems and recommends changing keys on a schedule.

It also quotes the warning in RFC 4107 that manual and automated key management offer very different features. Automated protocols confirm peer liveness, protect against replay and can negotiate algorithms, which manual keying cannot do. The database accommodates both, and a future specification to populate rows automatically is envisioned.
sections.eli5: Handing out secrets by hand is slow and easy to get wrong, so the notebook is built to work with hand-written entries and with machines that fill it in.

sections.title: The Three IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA established three registries. KeyTable Protocols is Specification Required, with entries giving the protocol name, a description of its protocol-specific info and a reference; it has no initial registrations. KeyTable KDFs and KeyTable AlgIDs are First Come First Served.

The initial KDF values are none, AES-128-CMAC and HMAC-SHA-1. The initial AlgID values are AES-128-CMAC, AES-128-CMAC-96 and HMAC-SHA-1-96. Both lists are based on the algorithms defined for TCP-AO.
sections.eli5: There are three public lists of names, so everybody uses the same words for the same protocols and tricks.
